comment: The quest as a graph. `start` names the first stage. Each stage carries the objective the tracker shows, the dialogue state every NPC switches to on entering it (a key into each npc's `dialogue` in npcs.json), the transitions that leave it, and optionally `enter` actions run on arrival. A transition fires `on` an event and may `do` actions, move `to` another stage, or both. Actions are the names src/quest-manager.js implements (QuestManager.actions); an `after` is a delay in ms. `tokens` are substituted into dialogue lines before they are shown. test/quest.mjs checks all of this against npcs.json, riddle.json, mystery.json, scene-config.json and index.html.
frameComment: PHASE 7 PROMOTED THE FRAME AND DELETED THE RIDDLE QUEST. Phase 1 wrote this graph under a `frame` key beside the three stages the page played (seek-keystone, present-keystone, gate-open) and the Keystone those stages talked about; both are gone, and what is left is the graph the mystery actually runs in. The riddle survived (#416) as the word-lock on the muniment room: `lock:muniment` opens it and `riddle:solved` does `openLock`, which unlocks the room in the engine and swings the leaf. `openGate` and `showVictory` went with the three stages, and so did `frame` itself: there is one graph in this file now.
events: talked:<npc> (an id in npcs.json's `cast`) when that conversation is stepped through to its end; lock:<id> when the player presses E at a word-locked door; riddle:solved when the overlay accepts the word; bell:<n> on the nth ring; clue:<id> when a clue lands; press:<npc>:<clue> when a press moves someone; ask:journal and ask:accuse when the player asks for the journal or for the Constable's judgement; accused:<who> and verdict:<class> when he gives it.

tokens.{ACCUSE}: Well. Have you a name for me, or do I write that he fell?

arrive.objective: The master mason is dead at the foot of the Chapel Tower stair. Find the Constable.
arrive.comment: The Constable stands over the body at Prime, which is where the player spawns, so this stage is one conversation long. His lines end in {ACCUSE} and nothing opens here: the first time he asks for a name the answer is the objective below, not the overlay. The word-lock is repeated in all three non-terminal stages because a door that is inert until the player has had a conversation on the other side of the castle reads as a broken door; test/plan-vs-scene.mjs pressed E at it before meeting anybody and found exactly that. The J key is here for the same reason.

investigate.objective: Learn what happened to Hywel ap Gruffudd before Vespers.
investigate.comment: The whole day. Three bells move the watch; the fourth is the Constable demanding an answer, and it is the only transition out of here that the player does not choose. `talked:constable` opens the accusation overlay rather than moving, because asking him is not the same as answering him: the move happens on `ask:accuse`, which src/mystery.js emits when an accusation is actually made.

accusing.objective: Name the one who killed him, or call it a fall.
accusing.comment: openAccusation is on `enter` and not on the bell's transition so that a save resumed here comes back to the overlay. A refusal emits ask:accuse and no verdict, so this stage has no ask:accuse transition at all: the overlay was never closed, and the manager writes the Constable's refusal line into the panel that is already open. The word-lock is repeated here because the ledger is still worth opening at Vespers.

full.objective: The Clerk hangs, the Steward is taken, and the lead is found in the town.
full.comment: NOT TERMINAL SINCE #537. The epilogue pane is up and the only thing on it is the button, which reads "The next morning" now and dispatches `day:2`. A verdict stage with no `day:2` transition gets the old button back and erases the save, so deleting this one line is how a verdict is made to end the game outright.

right.objective: The Clerk hangs. The Steward keeps his post.

A verdict stage with no `day:2` transition gets the old button back and erases the save, so deleting this one line is how a verdict is made to end the game outright.

morning.objective: Lauds, the morning after. Walk the castle, then take yourself to the King's inspector in the King's Hall.
morning.comment: One watch, no clues, no bell and no accusation. `applyDay` is on `enter` rather than on the transition into here so that a save resumed in this stage comes back to Lauds with the cast where the verdict put them, which is the same reason `accusing` carries `openAccusation` on `enter`. The word-lock is repeated for the reason the three day-one stages repeat it: a door that does nothing reads as a broken door, and the ledger is still worth opening on the morning after. `talked:inspector` is the only way out, and mystery.json's `day2.ends` names him; test/quest.mjs holds the two to each other.

end.comment: `applyDay` again, and not by accident: a save resumed straight into this stage has never run the morning, so without it the closing pane comes up over a castle still standing at Vespers with six people in the Great Hall. It is idempotent — `beginDay2` sets `day` to 2 and reads the same recorded verdict either way.
